summary: Extends the Alternate-Marking method to flows whose packets may take several different paths, so measurements work across multipoint-to-multipoint networks. It does this by grouping parts of the network into clusters and measuring at the cluster level. It obsoletes RFC 8889.

plainLanguage.summary: The Alternate-Marking method measures how much traffic is lost and how long it takes to cross a network, by marking packets and counting them at each measuring point. This document extends it to flows whose packets take several different routes, by splitting the network into clusters that can be measured one at a time.

questions: how to measure loss across multiple paths
how to measure packet loss on multipath flows
what is a cluster in alternate marking
subtitle: How to measure loss and delay across a flow whose packets travel along several different paths.

tldr.problem: The Alternate-Marking method measures one path between two points, so it cannot measure a flow whose packets are spread over several paths, which is what a multipoint-to-multipoint flow looks like.
tldr.mechanism: The method defines a monitoring network and then partitions it into clusters, small subnetworks where the number of packets entering equals the number leaving. Packet loss and delay are then computed per cluster, and a cluster can be combined with others for more or less detail.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9342 obsoletes RFC 8889 and adds recommendations for deployments that have one flag bit, two flag bits, or one flag bit plus hash-based packet selection.

today: RFC 9342 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8889, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It extends the Alternate-Marking method of RFC 9341 to multipoint-to-multipoint flows.

sections.title: Measuring Flows That Follow Several Paths
sections.content:
The Alternate-Marking Method, described in RFC 9341, applies to a point-to-point path. This document extends it to the most general case, a multipoint-to-multipoint path, and enables flexible and adaptive performance measurements in a managed network.

The Alternate-Marking methodology consists of splitting the packet flow into marking blocks, and the monitoring parameters are the packet counters and the timestamps for each marking period. Multipoint Alternate Marking aims to reduce these values and makes performance monitoring more flexible when a detailed analysis is not needed. Considering n measurement points and m monitored flows, the order of magnitude of the packet counters for each time interval is n*m*2, one per color.

The approach applies only to unicast flows and not to multicast. Broadcast, Unknown Unicast and Multicast traffic is not considered, because traffic replication is not covered. The method does apply to anycast flows, and Equal-Cost Multipath paths can also be monitored with this technique. The document is a methodology document: the mechanism used to transmit the counters and timestamps is out of scope. It assumes that blocks are created according to a fixed timer.
sections.plainLanguage: The older marking method works when every packet of a flow travels the same way between two points. This document covers the harder case where the packets are spread over several routes, which happens with load balancing, with several sources, or with several destinations.

sections.title: Monitoring Network, Cluster and Multipoint Metrics
sections.content:
The document keeps the basic terms of Alternate Marking and adds four. Multipoint Alternate Marking is the extension to RFC 9341 that is valid for multipoint-to-multipoint unicast flows, anycast and ECMP flows; it can also be called Clustered Alternate Marking. The flow definition is generalized: the identification fields are selected without any constraints, and the flow can be a multipoint-to-multipoint flow resulting from aggregate point-to-point flows. The monitoring network is the set of nodes that are the measurement points and the links that connect them; it depends on the flow definition, so it can represent a specific flow or the whole network topology as an aggregate of all the flows. A cluster is the smallest identifiable non-trivial subnetwork of the monitoring network graph that still satisfies the condition that the number of packets that go in is the same as the number that go out.

Multipoint metrics extend packet loss, delay and delay variation to multipoint flows. They can be computed on the basis of multipoint paths, so a measurement can be associated with a cluster, a combination of clusters, or the whole monitored network. For delay and delay variation they can also be defined on a single-packet basis, where the multipoint path is used to couple packets between the input and output nodes of that path.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ideas carry the document. The monitoring network is the part of the network being watched. A cluster is a piece of it that either sends in as many packets as it sends out, or shows the difference. The metrics are the usual loss and delay numbers, but they can be reported for a whole network, for one cluster, or for one packet.

sections.title: How a Flow Definition Shapes the Path
sections.content:
A unicast flow is identified by all the packets having a set of common characteristics. In general, a flow can be defined by a set of selection rules that match a subset of the packets processed by a network device. These rules specify a set of Layer 3 and Layer 4 header fields, the identification fields, and the relative values that must be found in matching packets.

The choice of identification fields directly affects the type of path the flow follows. A TCP 5-tuple usually identifies flows following either a single path or a point-to-point multipath in the case of load balancing. A single source address selects aggregate flows following a point-to-multipoint path, while a multipoint-to-point path can be the result of matching on a single destination address. When a selection rule and its reverse are used for bidirectional measurements, they can correspond to a point-to-multipoint path in one direction and a multipoint-to-point path in the opposite direction.

The flows to be monitored are selected at the monitoring points using packet selection rules, which can also change the pattern of the monitored network. The Alternate-Marking Method is applicable only to a single path, and partially to a one-to-one multipath, so the extension in this document also covers the most general multipoint-to-multipoint case, which embraces all the other patterns. The anycast flow is covered as well, since it is a special case of a unicast flow if routing is stable throughout the measurement period. An ECMP flow is in scope by definition, since it is a point-to-multipoint unicast flow.
sections.plainLanguage: What you count as one flow decides what shape the network takes. Counting full five-part TCP addresses gives one path. Counting everything from one source address gives a fan-out, and counting everything to one destination address gives a fan-in. The method here works for all of those shapes.

sections.title: Measuring Packet Loss and Delay
sections.content:
Since all the packets of the considered flow leaving the network have previously entered it, the number of packets counted by all the input nodes is always greater than or equal to the number counted by all the output nodes. The number of lost packets for one monitored flow in a single period is the number of packets counted by the input nodes minus the number counted by the output nodes, which is true for every packet flow in each marking period. The equation is applied per time interval and per flow, with the reference interval being the Alternate-Marking period.

Delay and delay variation follow the same reasoning. Delay measurements on the basis of multipoint paths mean that the delay value is representative of an entire multipoint path, and the average latency is measured as the difference between the weighted averages of the mean timestamps of the sets of output and input nodes, weighing the timestamps with the number of packets for each endpoint. Delay measurements on a single-packet basis use a multipoint path to couple packets between the input and output nodes of that path.

Single Marking based on the first or last packet of the interval does not work properly in a multipoint scenario, because it is not possible to recognize which path the first packet of each block takes. Double Marking works, but only through statistical means: by selecting only one packet with the second marking for each block, the measurement can be done for a single path in each marking period, and covering all paths means continuing over the following periods. Hash-based selection, which can work in a multipoint-to-multipoint path, is the option for monitoring all the paths of a multipoint path in the same marking period.
sections.plainLanguage: Loss is simple arithmetic: add up the packets that entered the part of the network you are measuring and subtract the packets that came out. For delay, the document offers a mean value for the whole path and a per-packet method; the per-packet method that relies on the first packet of each block does not work when packets split over several paths, so hash-based selection is used instead.

sections.title: Splitting the Network into Clusters
sections.content:
The equation of Section 4.2 determines the number of packets lost globally, using only the counters at the input and output nodes. It is also possible to use the counters at the other nodes to converge on the smallest identifiable subnetworks where the losses occur.

A cluster is a non-trivial subnetwork of the monitoring network graph that still satisfies the condition that the number of packets that go in is the same as the number that go out, if no packet loss occurs. According to this definition a cluster should contain all the arcs emanating from its input nodes and all the arcs terminating at its output nodes. This ensures that all the packets, and only those, exiting an input node can be counted again at the output node, whatever path they follow.

In a completely monitored network, where every network interface is monitored, each network device corresponds to a cluster and each physical link corresponds to two clusters, one for each device. Clusters can have different sizes depending on the flow-filtering criteria adopted. Sometimes clusters can be simplified: when two monitored interfaces are divided by a single router that has only those two interfaces, it is possible to consider a single measurement point instead of counting exactly twice, entering and leaving, because the internal packet loss of the router is then not of interest. Defining clusters on topological information can also make them applicable to all possible flows in the monitored network. In case of translation or encapsulation, the cluster properties must also be invariant.
sections.plainLanguage: A cluster is a piece of the network that is self-contained: whatever enters it either leaves it or gets lost inside it. Building clusters lets the operator find where the loss happened instead of only learning that the whole network lost packets. Clusters can be merged, since the same arithmetic holds for any connected group of them.

sections.title: Synchronization, Timing and the Guard Band
sections.content:
Timing matters, because out-of-order packets happen and have to be handled. In a multisource situation an additional issue appears: the egress nodes receive alternately marked packets in random order from different ingress nodes, and this must not affect the measurement. When a multipoint-to-multipoint path has more than one marking node, the measurement interval for describing the results is the interval of the marking node that is more aligned with the start of the measurement.

RFC 9341 describes two contributions to the timing constraints: the clock error between network devices and the network delay between the measurement points. In a multipoint environment there are more marking nodes marking traffic based on synchronized clock time, and different synchronization issues can make the marking batches of different lengths and offsets when they are mixed in a multipoint flow. The additional gap that results between the multiple sources can be incorporated into the maximum clock skew A.

The definition of the guard band d is then applicable, and is given by d = A + D_avg + 3*D_stddev, where A is the clock accuracy, D_avg is the average value of the network delay, and D_stddev is the standard deviation of the delay. The condition that must be satisfied for the method to function properly is that the available counting interval must be greater than zero, which means L - 2d > 0. This formula needs to be verified for each measurement point on the multipoint path, and the timing considerations are valid for both packet loss and delay measurements.
sections.plainLanguage: Every device has its own clock, so the marking blocks of different devices do not line up exactly. The document handles this with a guard band, a margin of time around each block that absorbs the clock error and the variation in network delay. The block has to be long enough that this margin fits on both sides, which is the condition L - 2d > 0.

sections.title: Deployment Choices and Network Zooming
sections.content:
Three deployments are possible, depending on how many flag bits are available for marking. With one flag, packet loss must be measured by applying the network clustering partition, and delay must be measured with the mean delay calculation representative of the multipoint path; a Single-Marking method based on the first or last packet of the interval cannot be applied. With two flags, packet loss must again be measured by applying the clustering partition, and delay should be measured on a single-packet basis with the Double-Marking method, with the mean delay calculation optionally used as a representative value. With one flag and hash-based selection, packet loss must be measured by applying the clustering partition, and hash-based selection must be used for delay measurement.

The choice also depends on the duration of the marking period, which affects the frequency of the measurement but cannot be freely chosen, on the type of data needed, since a single-packet basis needs two flags, and on the computational resources at the measurement points, since mean delay calculation may require more processing. The method must only be applied to controlled domains.

The framework also supports a closed-loop approach. The monitoring network can be considered as a whole or split into clusters, and a controller or network management system can start without examining the network in depth. When packet loss is measured or the delay is too high, the filtering criteria can be reconfigured to partition the network using clusters and combinations of clusters, localizing the problem and narrowing the analysis step by step up to a point-to-point flow. This approach is called network zooming, and it works either by changing the traffic filter to select more detailed flows or by activating new measurement points with more specified clusters. The document also notes that the framework helps traffic visualization, because it identifies which path or cluster a flow crosses.
sections.plainLanguage: How much you can measure depends on how many marking bits you have in the packet header. One bit gives you loss and an average delay; two bits let you time individual packets; one bit plus hash-based sampling also gives per-packet timing. The operator can then zoom in: start with the whole network and, when something looks wrong, narrow the view to the cluster where the problem is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This document specifies a method of performing measurements that does not directly affect Internet security or the applications that run on the Internet. However, implementation of the method must be mindful of security and privacy concerns, as explained in RFC 9341. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: The method itself does not change how traffic is delivered or what applications do. The security and privacy points to watch come from the underlying Alternate-Marking method that it extends.
